segments.text: For years, running AI at home came with one unwritten rule.
Big model, big GPU.
A 7 billion parameter model?
Sure, almost any decent machine can run that.
14 billion, we start checking specs.
70 billion?
Now we're spending real money.
And a model with over 100 billion parameters?
That lived in a data center.
Everyone knew it.
Then, people on Reddit started posting their speeds, and they were way higher than anyone
expected.
A hundred and twenty-five billion parameter model, running on a regular gaming PC.
Fast enough to actually chat with.
One person with two RTX 3090 GPUs said they were seeing over a hundred tokens per second.
Someone with an RTX 4080 Super said 40 to 60.
A 4090 owner said more than 140.
So, what changed? The GPUs didn't get any extra memory. The software just got much smarter
about using the memory they already have.
The project is called Strata. We'll walk through how it works, starting with the problem it's
trying to solve. A model is basically a giant list of numbers. We call them parameters. 125
billion parameter model has 125 billion of them. And to run the model, the GPU needs
fast access to all those numbers. The GPU keeps them in its own memory, called VRAM. VRAM is very
fast, but it's small. A typical gaming GPU has 12, 16 or maybe 24 gigabytes. Even after we shrink
a model this big, it's still bigger than that. But a gaming PC has a second kind of memory too,
regular system RAM. It's slower than VRAM, but there's a lot more of it. A well-built gaming
PC might have 64GB or more. So the old question was simple. Does the model fit in VRAM? If it
doesn't, we start making compromises. Slower speeds, worse quality, or giving up. Strata
tries something different. What if the GPU doesn't have to hold the whole model at once?
Strata is an open-source inference engine. Inference just means running a model to get
answers as opposed to training it. An inference engine is the software that loads the model
onto our hardware and does the actual work. If we've used llama CPP or VLLM, we've used one.
Those two are general purpose. They handle lots of different models.
Strata goes the other way. Right now it's built for one model, quen 3.8 flash next,
125 billion parameter model. Because it only has to care about one model, it can make bets that
a general tool can't. The project's claim is that an Nvidia GPU with 12GB of VRAM and
64GB of system RAM is enough to run it at tens of tokens per second. Quick note on that unit.
A token is a small chunk of text, about three quarters of a word. Tokens per second tells
us how fast the model writes. Most of us read at roughly five or six tokens a second,
so at fifty the model is writing far faster than we can read.
So how does it pull this off? There are three ideas and they stack on top of each other.
The first idea comes from the model itself. QEN 3.8 Flash Next is a mixture of experts
model or MOE. In a normal dense model, every parameter works on every token, all 125 billion
every single time. An MOE model is built differently. Inside it are lots of small specialist networks
called experts, a little component called the router looks at each token and picks which experts
should handle it. Everyone else sits that token out. In this model only about 6 billion of the
125 billion parameters are active for any one token. Say we run a company with 125,000 employees.
Any given task needs about 6,000 of them. We still need the whole company on the payroll
because we don't know which specialists the next task will want. But we don't need all of them
in the room at once. Strata takes advantage of that gap.
Let's stay with the company. Our GPU's VRAM is the meeting room. Small, fast, right where
the work happens. Our system RAM is the rest of the building. Much bigger, but a walk away.
Strata fills the meeting room with the specialists the model calls on most. Everyone else waits
in the building. When the router asks for someone who isn't in the room, Strata goes
and gets them. This is called expert caching. If we've seen the word cache anywhere else
in computing, it's the same idea. Keep what we use most in the fastest place.
One community benchmark on an RTX 4090 had about 12,000 of the model's 24,576 experts
sitting in GPU memory. The other half were in system RAM. And it still reported over
for 140 tokens per second on some workloads, so the GPU doesn't have to hold the whole
model. It only needs the parts we're using right now.
This works so well, partly because the model was built to wake only a small slice of itself.
It was already sparse, so Strata only has to decide where each piece should live. That's
also why Strata is so specialised. It leans on how this one model works.
Quick note before we keep going, if you like this kind of content, please subscribe.
I'll be covering the latest Frontier AI models, jargon free.
Ok, back to Strata.
Even with caching, 125 billion parameters is a lot of data.
So Strata also uses quantisation.
Each parameter is stored as a number.
Quantisation stores that number with fewer bits.
Less precision, much less memory.
It's like saving a photo as a smaller jpeg.
The file shrinks a lot and the picture still looks mostly fine.
again. Push it too far and we start to see the damage.
Strata offers several levels, with names like Q2.0, IQ2.xs, IQ3.xxs and IQ3.s. We don't
need to memorise them.
The two and the three roughly tell us how many bits each number gets. Fewer bits mean
smaller and faster, but possibly a little dumber.
That's why Strata gives us a menu, instead of one setting. The goal is to find the
where the model is small enough to run well without losing too much of its intelligence.
So how fast is it? Let's look at what the project reports for its own test machine,
an RTX 5070 with 12GB of VRAM and 64GB of RAM. On short conversations, it gets 93 tokens per second
at Q20, 79 at IQ2XS, 62 at IQ3XS and 53 at IQ3S. The fewer the bits, the faster it runs.
That's the quantisation trade-off showing up in real data.
It also reports prompt processing speed, which is how fast the model reads what we send it
before it starts writing, at up to 2,170 tokens per second.
Those numbers come from the project's own testing.
Speed depends on the GPU, the RAM, the CPU, the quantisation, the context length, and
what we're asking the model to do.
We should treat them as a best case, not a promise.
The community numbers are fun too. One person modified Strata to use an RTX 5080 and an RTX 4060 Ti together.
They reported about 143 tokens per second on code and 102 on pros, compared to roughly 28 with the 5080 alone.
Those are experiments, not standard benchmarks. Still, they show how far people are already pushing it.
Another thing Strata cares about is context length. The context window is how much text
the model can keep in mind at once. Our conversation, a pasted document, the whole code base. Long
context costs memory. While the model writes, it keeps notes on every token it has already
seen so it doesn't have to redo the work. Those notes are called the KV cache, and
the longer the conversation, the bigger they get.
Strata's benchmarks reach 128K tokens of context, and speeds there still land between
about 46 and 74 tokens per second. Its docs also describe experimental setups stretching
toward 384K and 512K. One community experiment tried around 256K on a 48GB RTX 4090D, a 16GB
RTX 5070 Ti and 128GB of RAM. What's it like to use? Strata comes with a local web interface,
and it exposes an OpenAI-compatible API at a local address, 127.0.0.1 Port 8080.
There's an anthropic-compatible endpoint too. OpenAI-compatible just means that any tool that
knows how to talk to the OpenAI API can be pointed at this address instead. That covers
coding agents, chat apps, python scripts and RAG apps, which let a model search our own documents.
The model becomes a local server on our own PC, and our prompts never leave the machine.
It runs on Windows 10 and 11, and on Linux. It needs an NVIDIA RTX GPU from the 20-50 series,
at least 12GB of VRAM, enough RAM with 64GB as the standard baseline, and about 80GB of free disk
space. On Windows, a file called starthere.bat walks us through picking the model, the quantisation,
and the context length. There's also a low RAM mode for machines with a strong GPU,
but less system memory. And if we run out of VRAM, we have options. A more aggressive quantisation,
more offloading to RAM, or a second GPU. Strata tries to work out the siblet for us.
Now for the limits, because the headline can mislead us. This doesn't mean any model this
size runs on any laptop. Strata is built around one model, and we still need a capable machine.
The speed of our RAM, the PCI Express link that experts travel across when they move from RAM to
the GPU, are SSD, and the GPU itself all change the experience. And fast for one person isn't
the same as fast for a crowd. Serving a thousand users at once means handling many requests at
the same time, which is a different problem. Engines like VLLM were built for it. Strata
isn't built for that. And it won't replace Llama CPP, which supports a huge range of models.
Strata's sweet spot fits in one sentence. We have a powerful gaming PC, and we want
to run a huge model on it.
We think the biggest story is what projects like Strata point to. Until now, the size
of our GPU's memory mostly decided what we could run at home.
Sparse models loosen that limit, and engines built around them loosen it even more.
The GPU becomes the fast workspace, and RAM holds the rest.
Say we build a gaming PC with 24GB of VRAM, 128GB of RAM and a fast SSD.
A few years ago we'd have called that a gaming rig.
Now we could also be a private AI machine.
We could run a big, open model with no cloud provider, point a coding agent at it, and
search our own documents without uploading them anywhere.
A hundred and twenty-five billion parameter model, running at dozens of tokens per second
on consumer hardware, would have sounded silly not long ago.
Now it's an engineering problem.
For a long time, the first question was how much VRAM we have.
Now there's a second question.
How well can our software use all the memory in the machine?
That second question may drive a lot of the next progress in local AI.
